content: The recommendations for the pharmacological treatment of hypertension in adults highlight the variability in patient and provider perspectives. Some patients value self-care applications, while others worry about potential harm to the patient-doctor relationship, particularly with the use of home-monitoring devices. In-depth interviews in the UK revealed concerns about clinical governance, privacy, and space limitations in community pharmacies for nurse and pharmacist prescribing. However, patients expressed fewer concerns about nurse-led management. A study in Scotland reported high satisfaction with pharmacist prescribing, though 65% of patients preferred consulting a doctor. Task-shifting in public healthcare systems may reduce health inequities by increasing access in underserved areas. Cost analyses suggest that community team-based approaches to hypertension management cost approximately $200 per person annually but result in significant cost savings by preventing cardiovascular disease (CVD) outcomes, with a median net cost of $65 per person annually. Pharmacist-led programs appear more cost-effective than nurse-led ones, with most cost-effectiveness estimates ranging between $3,888 and $24,000 per quality-adjusted life year (QALY). Only two studies exceeded $50,000/QALY. However, most cost data focus on self-monitoring rather than physician-led versus non-physician-led care. Lower salaries for non-physicians may reduce costs, assuming limited physician oversight is required. Collaborative physician-pharmacist systems have shown similar cost-effectiveness. In disaster and humanitarian settings, hypertension (HTN) is prevalent and poses significant challenges. Examples include conflicts in Syria and Iraq, the Great East Japan Earthquake, and Hurricane Katrina. HTN management in these settings is hindered by destroyed healthcare infrastructure, shortages of medical personnel and supplies, and high psychological stress. Armed conflicts are associated with increased cardiac morbidity and mortality, as well as elevated BP. Post-traumatic stress disorder and severe injuries are independent risk factors for HTN. There is no consensus on target BP or the best antihypertensive agents for disaster-related HTN, though long-acting calcium channel blockers (CCBs) are preferred for their metabolic neutrality and ability to reduce BP variability, a predictor of stroke. During the COVID-19 pandemic, HTN was identified as a significant risk factor for severe disease and mortality. Observational studies reported higher rates of HTN among hospitalized COVID-19 patients (50–56%). Concerns about the use of angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEis) and angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) arose due to their interaction with ACE2, the receptor for SARS-CoV-2. However, evidence suggests that ACEi/ARB use does not increase COVID-19 severity, and discontinuing these medications in high-risk patients may worsen outcomes. Most professional societies recommend continuing ACEis/ARBs in COVID-19 patients. Further research is needed to clarify the role of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) in COVID-19. Hypertension during pregnancy, including chronic HTN, gestational HTN, pre-eclampsia, and eclampsia, is a common and serious condition. It contributes to up to 10% of pregnancy-related deaths and increases long-term cardiovascular risks for both mother and fetus. HTN in pregnancy is diagnosed when BP is ≥140/90 mmHg on two occasions at least six hours apart. Chronic HTN is diagnosed before 20 weeks of gestation, while gestational HTN occurs at or after 20 weeks. Pharmacological treatment is recommended for severe HTN (systolic BP ≥160 mmHg or diastolic BP ≥105 mmHg). Preferred medications include methyldopa, beta-blockers (e.g., labetalol), CCBs (e.g., nifedipine), and hydralazine. ACEis, ARBs, and atenolol are contraindicated due to adverse fetal effects. Long-term follow-up is essential, as hypertensive pregnancy disorders significantly increase future cardiovascular risks. The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed guidelines for hypertension management, including in humanitarian crises. These guidelines emphasize the importance of early diagnosis, appropriate pharmacological treatment, and follow-up. Implementation is supported through WHO’s HEARTS technical package, which is being adapted for use in various countries. Future updates to the guidelines will consider emerging evidence and user needs. Identified research gaps include optimal BP thresholds for treatment initiation, cost-effectiveness of intensive treatment, and the role of combination therapy versus monotherapy. Further studies are needed to address these gaps, particularly in lowand middle-income countries.
